mainTopic: The seven חקירות: their source, how far they extend, a possible eighth question, and the source for התראה
overview: The משנה requires seven חקירות (questions to the witnesses), and the גמרא found them spread across three פסוקים. It explains that the shared word "היטב" creates a free גזירה שוה linking the three, so all seven questions apply to stoning and sword cases even though the cases differ. Strangling and burning cases are then added by a קל וחומר. Because רבי שמעון holds that burning is harsher, רב יהודה finds one spare word in the פסוקים to teach about burning. רבי אבהו suggests the spare word might add an eighth question instead, and the גמרא tests possible candidates. Next comes the debate between רבי יוסי and the חכמים over whether the court asks every time question even when it seems pointless. A ברייתא then lists the essential questions in murder and idol worship cases. Finally, עולא begins to show from the word "וראה" that the Torah requires התראה, an argument that finishes on the next amud.

steps.title: Maybe each case keeps only its own questions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: why not say each case gets only the חקירות written in its own verse?
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe each one is just as it is written? Because if all seven questions applied everywhere, the Torah should have written them all in one place!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on combining the questions from three different verses into one set of seven for every capital case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each verse lists only some of the questions. The challenge says that if the Torah wanted all seven in every case, it would have written them together. Writing them in separate places suggests each case gets only its own.

keyTerms.meaning: But maybe say (opens a challenge with a different reading)

phrases.english: But say: each one is as it is written?
phrases.notes: He means each of the three cases gets only the questions listed in its own פסוק.

phrases.english: For if so,
let the Merciful One write them in one place!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier count of seven חקירות gathered from three verses.
steps.kashyaTarget: Combining the questions from three verses into one set of seven for all capital cases.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If all seven applied everywhere, the Torah would have written them together; writing them separately suggests each case stays separate.

steps.title: Verses written alike count as written together
steps.stepSummary: Since the verses are worded alike, they are learned from each other, so it is as if they were written in one place.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since they are all written in the same way, we learn one from the other. And once we learn them from each other, it is as if they were written in one place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the three verses are connected, so their questions combine into one set.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah does not need to write everything in one spot. When verses use matching wording, each one teaches about the others. That linkage works as if all seven questions were written together.

keyTerms.meaning: Together with each other (here: in matching wording)
It is like, it is considered

phrases.english: Since they are all written alike,
they are learned from one another,
and since they are learned from one another,
it is as if it were written in one place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Linking the verses so they act as one source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each case gets only its own questions, since they were written apart.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verses teach about each other, so all seven questions apply to all three cases.

steps.title: But the three cases are not alike
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the three cases are different from each other, so how can one learn from another? It gives a memory aid for the differences.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they are not similar to each other! (Memory aid: escapes, sword, warning.)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of step 2, saying the three cases are too different to learn from one another. It gives a short memory aid, and the next step will spell out the differences.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Learning one case from another normally needs the cases to be comparable. If each case has a special feature the others lack, the comparison breaks down. The three code words point to the three differences explained next.

keyTerms.meaning: A warning given before the sin

phrases.english: But they are not similar to each other?
(Mnemonic: escapes, sword, warning.)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the three verses can be learned from one another.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Different cases cannot be compared to each other, and these three cases each have a unique feature.

steps.title: The three differences spelled out
steps.stepSummary: Each case has something the other two lack: עיר הנדחת loses its property, idol worship is by stoning, and עדים זוממין need no warning.
steps.simpleTranslation: עיר הנדחת is not like the other two, because in those their money escapes. Idol worship is not like the other two, because those are by the sword. עדים זוממין are not like the other two, because those need a warning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the memory aid, showing how each of the three cases differs from the other two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In עיר הנדחת even the property is destroyed, while in the others the money is spared. Idol worship is punished by stoning, while the others are by the sword. The other two sins need a warning, but עדים זוממין are never warned. So no single case can stand in for the others.

keyTerms.meaning: A city led astray into idol worship

phrases.aramaic: עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת לְהָנָךְ תַּרְתֵּי לָא דָּמְיָא,
phrases.english: An idolatrous city is not similar to those two,
since their money escapes.
phrases.notes: In the other two cases the property is spared; in עיר הנדחת the property is destroyed too.

phrases.aramaic: עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה לְהָנָךְ תַּרְתֵּי לָא דָּמְיָא,
phrases.english: Idol worship is not similar to those two,
since they are by the sword.

phrases.aramaic: עֵדִים זוֹמְמִין לְהָנָךְ תַּרְתֵּי לָא דָּמְיָא,
phrases.english: Plotting witnesses are not similar to those two,
since they require a warning.

steps.triggerLanguage: עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת לְהָנָךְ תַּרְתֵּי לָא דָּמְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the challenge given in short form in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: Learning the three cases from one another.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each case has a unique feature, so any comparison between them can be broken.

steps.title: The link is the shared word "היטב"
steps.stepSummary: The cases are learned from each other through a גזירה שוה on the word "היטב", not through similar cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn them from each other through "היטב" and "היטב".
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the link does not come from the cases being alike. It comes from a גזירה שוה, the same word appearing in each verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזירה שוה is a tradition that links two verses through a shared word. It does not depend on the cases being similar. So the differences listed in step 4 do not automatically cancel it.

keyTerms.meaning: Well, thoroughly (the shared word in the verses)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא is saying the cases are similar after all. It agrees they are different. It is saying the link comes from a shared word, which works even between different cases.

phrases.english: We learn from one another through "diligently" and "diligently,"
phrases.notes: The word היטב appears in all three פסוקים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 3 and 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the basis of the link from similar cases to a גזירה שוה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The cases are compared because they are alike, so differences break the link.
steps.terutzMaskana: The link is a גזירה שוה on "היטב", which does not rely on the cases being alike.

steps.title: The גזירה שוה must be free
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that this גזירה שוה must be מופנה (free), because otherwise the differences could still break it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the גזירה שוה must be free. Because if it is not free, it can be refuted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a condition: the answer only works if the word "היטב" is extra. This sets up the next step, which shows that it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the linking word is needed for its own simple meaning, the differences between the cases can still knock down the גזירה שוה. Only if the word is extra, a free word, is the link strong enough to ignore the differences.

keyTerms.meaning: A link between verses through a shared word
Free, extra; not needed for its simple meaning

phrases.english: And the verbal analogy is free.
phrases.notes: Free means the word is extra in its own פסוק, as if left there just to teach the link.

phrases.english: For if it is not free, it can be refuted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a condition to the answer of step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A גזירה שוה can stand up against differences between the cases only if its word is free (מופנה).

steps.title: "היטב" is clearly free
steps.stepSummary: It cannot be refuted, because the word is free: the Torah could have written "ודרשו וחקרו" without "היטב", so the change shows it is there for the link.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it cannot be refuted, because the words are free. Since the Torah could have written "and they shall inquire and investigate," and instead changed its wording to "היטב," learn from this that the word is there to be free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves that "היטב" is an extra word, so the גזירה שוה stands. The next step challenges this proof for the עיר הנדחת verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah could have used plain verbs like "ודרשו וחקרו." Using the word "היטב" instead is an unusual choice, which shows the word is there to create the link. So the גזירה שוה is free, and the differences from step 4 cannot break it.

keyTerms.meaning: And the verse changed its wording

steps.whatToRemember: The three verses are linked by a free גזירה שוה on "היטב", so the differences between the cases do not matter.

phrases.english: Not so; they are indeed free.
phrases.notes: He means: no, it can't be knocked down, because the words really are extra.

phrases.english: Since it could have written "and they shall inquire and investigate,"
and the verse changed its wording with "diligently,"
learn from it that it is there to be free.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fulfills the condition set in step 6 by proving the word is free.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe "היטב" is needed for its plain meaning, so the differences could break the link.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah changed its wording to "היטב", so the word is free and the גזירה שוה cannot be refuted.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The free גזירה שוה of "היטב" joins the three verses, so all seven חקירות apply in all three cases.

steps.title: The word is only free in two of the three verses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that "היטב" is extra in the פסוקים of idol worship and עדים זוממין, but not in the פסוק of עיר הנדחת, where every word is used.
steps.simpleTranslation: But still, the word is free on only one side! Granted, in these two cases it is free, because the Torah could have written the verse without it. But in עיר הנדחת, what else could the Torah have written? All the words are written there!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 7. It says the extra-word argument works for two of the cases, but not for עיר הנדחת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 7, "היטב" was called extra because the Torah could have written just "ודרשו וחקרו". But in the פסוק of עיר הנדחת, the Torah already writes all three verbs together with "היטב", so there is no shorter version to point to. That means the word is not clearly free on both sides of the link.

keyTerms.meaning: On one side only; free in some of the places but not all

phrases.english: But still, it is free on only one side!
Granted, in these two it is free,
phrases.notes: "These two" are idol worship and עדים זוממין.

phrases.english: because it could have written it differently.
But the עיר הנדחת,
what could it have written?
All of them are already written!
phrases.notes: There the פסוק says "ודרשת וחקרת ושאלת היטב", so all the verbs are already there (דברים 13:15).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 7 by showing it does not fit the עיר הנדחת verse.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 7 that "היטב" is free in every verse
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The 'could have written it shorter' argument fails in עיר הנדחת, where every verb already appears, so the word looks needed there.

steps.title: Even in עיר הנדחת the word is extra
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that in עיר הנדחת the Torah could have used a doubled verb like "דרוש תדרוש". Choosing "היטב" instead shows the word is there to be free.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too the word is free. The Torah could have written "you shall surely inquire" or "you shall surely investigate". Since the verse changed its wording and used "היטב", learn from it that the word is there to be free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 8. It shows that "היטב" is extra even in the עיר הנדחת verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual Torah way to stress a verb is to double it ("דרוש תדרוש"). Here the Torah stressed it with a different word, "היטב". That change in style tells us the word is there for the גזירה שוה, so the link is free on all sides and cannot be broken by the differences between the cases.

keyTerms.meaning: You shall surely inquire (a doubled verb for emphasis)
The verse changed its way of speaking
To make it free (for a גזירה שוה)

steps.whatToRemember: "היטב" is free in all three פסוקים, so the גזירה שוה stands. Stoning (idol worship) and sword (עיר הנדחת) cases both need the full questioning of the witnesses.

phrases.english: There too, it is indeed free,
since it could have written
"you shall surely inquire" or "you shall surely investigate,"
and the verse changed its wording by using "diligently"
learn from this that it is there to be free.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the verse closely: shows a different way the Torah could have written it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: In עיר הנדחת every word is needed, so "היטב" is not free there.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah could have stressed the verb by doubling it. Using "היטב" instead shows the word is free there too.

steps.title: Strangling and burning cases learned by a קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: Strangling cases learn the questioning rule by a קל וחומר from stoning and sword cases. Burning cases learn it by a קל וחומר from stoning cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the rule comes to those killed by strangling through a קל וחומר from those stoned and those killed by the sword. And it comes to those killed by burning through a קל וחומר from those stoned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גזירה שוה only covered stoning and sword deaths. Now the גמרא extends the questioning rule to the other two death penalties, strangling and burning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Strangling is a lighter death than both stoning and sword. If witnesses must be fully questioned even for the harsher deaths, all the more so for the lighter one. Burning is learned only from stoning, because burning is treated as lighter than stoning but not lighter than the sword.

keyTerms.meaning: A 'how much more so' argument, from a harsher case to a lighter one or the reverse
Those put to death by strangling
Those put to death by stoning
Those put to death by the sword
Those put to death by burning

steps.confusionAlert: Burning is learned only from stoning, not from the sword. This step assumes stoning is harsher than burning, and the very next step questions that.

phrases.english: And those strangled are learned by a קל וחומר
from those stoned and those killed by the sword,
and those burned are learned by a קל וחומר from those stoned.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָתוּ נֶחְנָקִין בְּקַל וָחוֹמֶר מִנִּסְקָלִין וּמִנֶּהֱרָגִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the גזירה שוה from steps 5 to 9 and extends its rule to the remaining death penalties.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Strangling cases get the questioning rule by a קל וחומר from stoning and sword. Burning cases get it by a קל וחומר from stoning.

steps.title: The burning argument fails for רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The קל וחומר for burning works for the רבנן, who hold that stoning is harsher. But רבי שמעון holds that burning is harsher, so how does it work for him?
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for the רבנן, who say stoning is the harsher death. But according to רבי שמעון, who says burning is harsher, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the burning part of step 10. The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קל וחומר only works if the case you learn from is the harsher one. For רבי שמעון, burning is harsher than stoning. So learning burning from stoning by a 'how much more so' argument falls apart, and the burning cases are left without a source.

phrases.english: This works well according to the Rabbis
who say stoning is more severe,
but according to Rabbi Shimon
who says burning is more severe,
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the burning half of the קל וחומר in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The קל וחומר that learns burning from stoning
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר needs the source case to be harsher. For רבי שמעון, burning is harsher than stoning, so the argument does not work.

steps.title: A new word count: eleven words, one left over
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה finds two more words, אמת and נכון, in both פסוקים. That makes eleven words: seven for the seven חקירות, three for the גזירה שוה, and one extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב יהודה said: "And behold it is true, the matter is certain" (in one פסוק), and "And behold it is true, the matter is certain" (in the other פסוק). Now there are eleven. Seven teach the seven questions. Take away three for the גזירה שוה, and one is left over.
steps.whatsHappening: The question from step 11 still stands, so the גמרא says "rather" and brings a new way to count the words. This new count leaves one extra word free to teach something.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words אמת and נכון appear in both פסוקים. That adds four words to the seven already counted, for a total of eleven. After seven go to the seven questions and three go to the גזירה שוה, one word is left over. That spare word is what the next step will use to answer the problem about burning cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It drops the earlier approach and brings a new one.
"True, certain": the two extra words found in the פסוקים

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Yehuda said:
"And behold it is true, the matter is certain"
"And behold it is true, the matter is certain"
phrases.notes: דברים 17:4. The two words appear in both פסוקים, so that is four more words added to the seven already counted.

phrases.english: So there are eleven.
Seven for the seven questions;
take away three for the gezeira shava;
one is left over for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty of step 11 by replacing the earlier word count with a new one that leaves a spare word.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New derivation that frees up an extra word
steps.terutzHavaAmina: For רבי שמעון there was no way to include burning cases, since the קל וחומר from stoning does not work for him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The new count leaves one extra word, which can teach the rule directly.

steps.title: What the extra word teaches for each opinion
steps.stepSummary: For רבי שמעון the extra word includes burning cases. For the רבנן, the Torah writes it out even though a קל וחומר already teaches it.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רבי שמעון, the extra word comes to include those who are burned. For the רבנן, it is a case where something that could be learned from a קל וחומר is still written out by the פסוק anyway.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the one leftover word does, according to each side of the argument about which death is harsher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון cannot use the קל וחומר, so for him the spare word is the source that burning cases also need the seven questions. The רבנן already have the קל וחומר. For them the extra word is not wasted, because the Torah sometimes writes out a rule even when logic could have taught it.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who are put to death by burning
The פסוק took the trouble to write it out

steps.whatToRemember: The one spare word teaches that burning cases also need the seven questions. For רבי שמעון it is the real source. For the רבנן it is the Torah spelling out what a קל וחומר already teaches.

phrases.english: According to Rabbi Shimon, it comes to include those who are burned.
According to the Rabbis,
a matter that can be learned through a kal vachomer
the verse still takes the trouble and writes it out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the spare word from step 12 to answer the question of step 11 for both opinions.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigns the extra word a role under each opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The spare word seems either needed only by רבי שמעון or wasted for the רבנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: It includes burning cases for רבי שמעון, and for the רבנן it spells out what the קל וחומר teaches.

steps.title: Why not an eighth question?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו waves off the answer: maybe the spare word teaches an eighth question instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו scoffed at this: say instead that the extra word comes to add an eighth question!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו challenges how the spare word was used. He suggests it might teach something else completely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If one extra word is free, nothing forces us to say it is about burning cases. It could just as well add another question to the list, which would make eight.

keyTerms.meaning: Scoffs at, waves off (literally, waves the hand)

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu scoffed at this:
Say it comes to add eight questions!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the use of the spare word in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: Using the spare word for burning cases
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A free word could just as easily add an eighth question.

steps.title: Is there even an eighth question?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether an eighth question even exists.
steps.simpleTranslation: And is there such a thing as eight questions?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי אבהו. What eighth question could there possibly be?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבהו's challenge only works if there is a real eighth question left to add. If no such question exists, his point falls away.

phrases.english: And are there eight questions?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the premise of רבי אבהו's challenge.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether any eighth question exists that the spare word could teach.

steps.title: The eighth question: what point in the hour
steps.stepSummary: Yes, there could be one: asking at what point within the hour the act happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why not? There is room to add the question "at what point in the hour?"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that an eighth question really is possible. The witnesses could be asked exactly when within the hour it happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual questions include which hour. A more exact question would be at what part of that hour. So רבי אבהו's suggestion has something real behind it.

keyTerms.meaning: At what point within the hour

phrases.english: Why not?
There is room to add: at what point in the hour.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The eighth question would be: at what point within the hour.

steps.title: A ברייתא mentions eight questions
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the witness was checked with eight questions, which backs up the idea.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is also taught so in a ברייתא: they would check him with eight questions.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that really does speak of eight questions, which supports רבי אבהו's suggestion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An eighth question is not just a guess. A teaching of the תנאים already counts eight. This makes רבי אבהו's challenge stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is also taught so in a ברייתא

phrases.english: And it is also taught so:
They would check him with eight questions.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the eighth question proposed in step 16.
steps.raayaObject: That there is such a thing as eight questions
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: "They would check him with eight questions"

steps.title: The eighth question makes no sense if witnesses err by half an hour
steps.stepSummary: Asking for the exact point in the hour makes sense if witnesses are exact, or off only a little. It does not make sense for the views that they can be off by half an hour or more.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for אביי's explanation of רבי מאיר, who says a person does not make any mistake at all. It also works for the other version, which says a person is off a little. But for אביי's explanation of רבי יהודה, who says a person can be off by half an hour, and for רבא, who says people are off by a lot, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a hard question about the eighth question. For some views about how far witnesses can be off on the time, asking which part of the hour is pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If witnesses are assumed exact, or only slightly off, then two witnesses who disagree about the part of the hour really do contradict each other. But if a person can be off by half an hour or more, such a difference is just an honest mistake. Then the question would prove nothing. The next step answers by proposing a different eighth question.

keyTerms.meaning: What is there to say? (a hard question with no ready answer)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not saying the eighth question is wrong for everyone. It only fits the views that treat witnesses as exact or nearly exact about the time.

phrases.english: This works well for Abaye's explanation of Rabbi Meir,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: אֵין אָדָם טוֹעֶה וְלֹא כְּלוּם,
phrases.english: who says: a person does not make any mistake at all,
and also for the other version, which says:
a person is off a little; it works well.
But for Abaye's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda,
who says: a person can be off by half an hour,
and for Rava, who says: people are off by a lot,
what is there to say?
phrases.notes: For these views, a difference about the part of the hour is just an honest mistake, so asking it proves nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the eighth question proposed in step 16 and supported in step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The eighth question, "at what point in the hour"
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If witnesses can be off by half an hour or more, a difference about the exact part of the hour is an honest mistake. Then the question cannot catch false witnesses and has no use.

steps.title: A new try: asking which year within the jubilee
steps.stepSummary: Since asking about the exact point in the hour does not fit every view, the גמרא suggests a different eighth question: in which year of the יובל did it happen?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the extra word comes to add the question: in which year of the jubilee cycle did it happen?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the 'point in the hour' idea and offers a different candidate for the eighth question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 showed that asking about the exact point in the hour only works for some views on how exact witnesses are. So the גמרא looks at the other end of the time scale: the big 50-year cycle. Maybe the eighth question asks which of the 50 years it was.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; dropping the last idea for a new one
To add or include something extra
In which number; at what count

phrases.english: Rather, it comes to add
in which year of the jubilee.
phrases.notes: Literally 'in how many in the יובל': which of its 50 years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the eighth question from step 16 after step 18 showed it does not fit all views.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Offers a different candidate for the eighth question
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The eighth question is about the exact point within the hour.
steps.terutzMaskana: Maybe the eighth question is which year of the יובל it was.

steps.title: That is the same as asking which seven-year period
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea: asking the year within the יובל is not really new, since the court already asks which שבוע and which year.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is the same as 'in which seven-year period'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the suggestion from step 19 by showing it adds nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court already asks which שבוע (seven-year period) and which year inside it. From those two answers you already know which year of the יובל it was. So this cannot be a separate eighth question.

keyTerms.meaning: That is the same thing as
Here: a seven-year period (שמיטה cycle), not a week

phrases.english: That is the same as 'in which seven-year period'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the suggestion of step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that 'which year of the יובל' is an eighth question
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It is already covered by asking which שבוע plus which year, so it adds nothing.

steps.title: Another try: asking which jubilee
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the eighth question could be: in which יובל cycle did it happen, this one or an earlier one?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it comes to add the question: in which jubilee did it happen?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers one more candidate for the eighth question, one level bigger than before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Knowing the שבוע and the year only tells you the spot inside a 50-year cycle. It does not tell you which 50-year cycle. So asking 'which יובל' really is new information.

phrases.english: Rather, it comes to add 'in which jubilee.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fixes the problem raised in step 20 by moving to a truly new question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Offers a new, non-overlapping eighth question
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The eighth question is which year of the יובל, but that overlaps with the שבוע question.
steps.terutzMaskana: The eighth question could be which יובל cycle, which is not covered by anything else.

steps.title: Why the other side needs no 'which jubilee' question
steps.stepSummary: The other side, who holds there are only seven questions, says once the witness names the שבוע, nobody needs to ask which יובל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other side? Once he said in which seven-year period, there is no need to ask in which jubilee.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the opinion that there are only seven questions does not accept 'which יובל' as an eighth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a witness names the שבוע, everyone assumes he means the current יובל. No one would think he is talking about something from over 50 years ago. So asking 'which יובל' is not needed, and the count stays at seven.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other side (how does he answer?)

steps.whatToRemember: There could be an eighth question ('which יובל'), but the view of seven questions says it is not needed, because naming the שבוע already points to the current יובל.

phrases.english: And the other side?
phrases.notes: The opinion that there's no eighth question: how does it deal with 'which יובל'?

phrases.english: Since he said in which seven-year period,
there is no need to ask in which jubilee.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the seven-question view answers the suggestion of step 21.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects 'which יובל' as a needed eighth question, according to the seven-question view
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The question is pointless, since naming the שבוע already means the current יובל.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: why ask about years if he said 'last night'?
steps.stepSummary: Turning to רבי יוסי in the משנה, a ברייתא shows him challenging the חכמים: if the witness says the killing was last night, why ask about the שבוע, year, month and date?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'רבי יוסי says.' It was taught: רבי יוסי said to the Sages: By your view, if someone comes and says 'He killed him last night,' should the judge ask him: In which seven-year period? In which year? In which month? On what day of the month?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new section of the משנה, רבי יוסי's view, and brings a ברייתא where he argues against the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי holds the court only needs day, hour and place. He shows how strange the חכמים' rule looks: if the witness says 'last night,' asking about the year and the seven-year cycle is silly. The point is that the big time questions are not always needed.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוסי is not saying the date does not matter. He is saying the extra questions are pointless when the witness already gave a time that makes them obvious.

phrases.english: 'Rabbi Yosei says.'

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר לָהֶם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי לַחֲכָמִים:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Yosei said to the Sages:
By your view, one who comes and says
'He killed him last night' — does one say to him
'In which seven-year period?' 'In which year?'
'In which month?' 'On what day of the month?'

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר לָהֶם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי לַחֲכָמִים: לְדִבְרֵיכֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the dispute in the משנה between רבי יוסי and the חכמים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The חכמים' rule that all seven questions are always asked
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: When the witness says 'last night,' questions about the year and cycle are pointless, so the rule cannot be required every time.

steps.title: The חכמים answer back: what if he said 'just now'?
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים turn the same argument on רבי יוסי: if the witness says the killing happened just now, why ask the day, hour or place?
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: By your view, if someone comes and says 'He killed him just now,' should the judge ask him: On which day? At which hour? In which place?
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים answer רבי יוסי by showing his own rule has the same problem in an even more extreme case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the witness says 'just now,' even רבי יוסי's three questions seem pointless. Yet רבי יוסי still asks them. So the same is true for the חכמים: the questions are asked as a fixed rule, even when the answer seems obvious.
steps.whatToRemember: Both sides admit the questions can look pointless in some cases. The חכמים use this to show that the questions are a fixed rule, asked even when the answer seems clear.

phrases.english: They said to him: By your view,
one who comes and says 'He killed him just now,'
does one say to him 'On which day?'
'At which hour?' 'In which place?'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: לִדְבָרֶיךָ, מִי שֶׁבָּא וְאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The חכמים turn רבי יוסי's argument from step 23 back against him.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי's argument that pointless questions should not be required
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By his logic, even day, hour and place would be pointless when the witness says 'just now', yet he still requires them.

steps.title: The חכמים: we ask all the questions anyway, like רבי שמעון בן אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים answer their own counter-challenge. Even when a question is not really needed, the court still asks it, following רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. So the same answer works for the 'last night' case too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, even though it is not needed, we still press all the questions on the witness, like רבי שמעון בן אלעזר taught. Here too, even though it is not needed, we press them on him, like רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים finish their reply to רבי יוסי. They say the court asks every standard question even when it seems pointless, so רבי יוסי's challenge about 'last night' does not hurt them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 23 רבי יוסי asked why the חכמים ask about the שבוע, year and month if the witness said 'last night.' In step 24 the חכמים showed that רבי יוסי has the same problem with 'just now.' Here they give the answer that covers both cases: the court always asks the full list, because extra questions help catch lying witnesses, as רבי שמעון בן אלעזר taught.

keyTerms.meaning: Even though it is not needed
We load it onto him (we press the witness with these questions)

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא צָרִיךְ,
phrases.english: Rather, even though it is not needed,

phrases.aramaic: רָמֵינַן עֲלֵיהּ כִּדְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר.
phrases.english: we press it on him, in line with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
phrases.notes: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר taught that the court keeps moving witnesses around with many questions to try to trip them up.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי, אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא צָרִיךְ,
phrases.english: Here too, even though it is not needed,
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the 'last night' case that רבי יוסי challenged us with.

phrases.aramaic: רָמֵינַן עֲלֵיהּ כִּדְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר.
phrases.english: we press it on him, in line with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא צָרִיךְ, רָמֵינַן עֲלֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the חכמים' reply. After turning the challenge back on רבי יוסי, they give the answer that settles both cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rule that all standard questions are asked even when unnecessary
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the witness said 'last night,' asking the שבוע, year and month seems pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The court asks every standard question anyway, to press the witnesses, following רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: 'last night' is common, 'just now' is rare
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains how רבי יוסי would defend himself. Testimony that someone killed 'last night' is common, so the questions are designed with it in mind. Testimony that someone killed 'just now' is rare, so the questions are not designed for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what would רבי יוסי say? 'He killed him last night' is common in most testimonies. 'He killed him just now' is not common in most testimonies.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how רבי יוסי escapes the חכמים' counter-challenge. The standard list of questions is built around the usual kind of testimony, not the rare kind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים argued that רבי יוסי's own questions (day, hour, place) are pointless when the witness says 'just now.' רבי יוסי answers that 'just now' almost never happens, so the court's fixed questions do not need to fit it. But 'last night' happens all the time, so a fixed list of questions should fit it. That is why he objects to the חכמים' extra questions about the שבוע, year and month.

phrases.english: And רבי יוסי?
'He killed him last night' is common in most testimonies,
'He killed him just now' is not common in most testimonies.

steps.whatToRemember: The debate between רבי יוסי and the חכמים ends here. The חכמים say all the questions are asked anyway, to press the witnesses. רבי יוסי says the fixed questions only need to fit the common case ('last night'), not the rare case ('just now').
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי יוסי's defense against the counter-challenge from step 24, which the חכמים used in step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between a common case and a rare case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוסי's questions (day, hour, place) seem just as pointless for 'just now' as the חכמים' questions are for 'last night.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The fixed list of questions is built for common testimony. 'Last night' is common and must be considered. 'Just now' is rare and can be ignored.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the essential questions in a murder case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next words of the משנה, 'Do you recognize him?', and brings a ברייתא listing the essential questions: who was killed, whether there was a warning, whether the killer accepted it, and whether he killed right after it.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Do you recognize him?' The Rabbis taught: Do you recognize him? Did he kill a non-Jew? Did he kill a Jew? Did you warn him? Did he accept the warning? Did he give himself over to death? Did he kill within the time it takes to say a short phrase?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה and brings a ברייתא that spells out the essential questions the court asks in a murder case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the discussion was about questions of time and place. Now the ברייתא lists questions about the substance of the crime: who the victim was, and whether a proper התראה (warning) was given, accepted, and followed right away by the act. Each one checks a condition needed before the court can give a death sentence.

keyTerms.meaning: A warning given before the crime
He gave himself over to death (he accepted that he would be killed for it)
Within the time it takes to say a short phrase

phrases.english: 'Do you recognize him?'
The Rabbis taught: Do you recognize him?
Did he kill a non-Jew? Did he kill a Jew?
Did you warn him? Did he accept the warning on himself?
Did he give himself over to death?
Did he kill within the time it takes to say a short phrase?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the time-and-place questions are settled, the גמרא opens a new topic: the essential questions from the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a murder case the court asks: do you recognize him, whom did he kill, was he warned, did he accept the warning and agree to die, and did he act right after the warning.

steps.title: The ברייתא continues: questions for an idol worshipper
steps.stepSummary: For someone accused of עבודה זרה, the court asks which idol he served (such as פעור or מרקוליס) and how he served it: by sacrifice, burning incense, pouring a drink offering, or bowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: For one who worships idols: Whom did he worship? Did he worship פעור? Did he worship מרקוליס? And how did he worship? By slaughtering? By burning incense? By pouring a drink offering? By bowing down?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and gives the essential questions for a different capital crime, עבודה זרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like murder, idol worship needs exact details before a death sentence. The court checks which idol it was and which act of worship was done, because the testimony must clearly describe a punishable act of worship.

keyTerms.meaning: Slaughtering a sacrifice, burning incense, pouring a drink offering

phrases.english: One who worships idols:
Whom did he worship?
Did he worship פעור? Did he worship מרקוליס?
And how did he worship?
By slaughtering a sacrifice? By burning incense?
By pouring a drink offering? By bowing down?

steps.whatToRemember: Besides time and place, the court must check the core details of the crime: in murder, who was killed and whether a proper התראה was given; in עבודה זרה, which idol and which act of worship.
steps.triggerLanguage: הָעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה. אֶת מִי עָבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, moving from murder to idol worship.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In an idol worship case the court asks which idol was worshipped and how: by sacrifice, incense, drink offering, or bowing.

steps.title: עולא brings a פסוק as the source for forewarning
steps.stepSummary: עולא asks where the תורה teaches התראה and answers with the פסוק about a man who takes his sister and 'sees' her nakedness.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: Where does the תורה teach that a sinner must be warned? From the פסוק: 'And a man who takes his sister, his father's daughter or his mother's daughter, and sees her nakedness.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings עולא, who gives a source in the תורה for the rule that a person must be warned before he can be punished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 27 listed 'was he warned?' as one of the court's questions. Now עולא shows that this requirement comes from the תורה itself. He points to the word 'וראה', and the next steps explain why that word teaches about warning.

keyTerms.meaning: Forewarning: telling the person before he sins that it is forbidden and what the punishment is
From where? Used to ask for a source
And he sees. This is the key word עולא builds on

phrases.english: Ulla said:
From where in the Torah do we learn forewarning?
As it says: "And a man who takes his sister,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 20:17. The same פסוק ends by saying they are punished with כרת.

phrases.english: his father's daughter or his mother's daughter,
and sees her nakedness."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר עוּלָּא: מִנַּיִין לְהַתְרָאָה מִן הַתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a source in the תורה for the warning requirement listed in the ברייתא of step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The requirement of התראה is learned from the word 'וראה' in ויקרא 20:17.

steps.title: Does the sin really depend on seeing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק mentions seeing, since the sin is the forbidden act and not looking.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does the matter really depend on seeing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the plain reading of 'and sees.' The sin is the forbidden relationship, so why would the פסוק make it depend on seeing?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not an attack on עולא. It sets up his proof. Because 'seeing' cannot be the real condition of the sin, the word must be teaching something else.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? An opening for a question that expects 'no'

phrases.english: Is that to say the matter depends on seeing?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the literal meaning of the word 'וראה' from the פסוק quoted in step 29.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain meaning of 'וראה' in the פסוק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The sin is the forbidden act and not seeing, so reading 'sees' literally makes no sense.

steps.title: 'Seeing' means being shown the reason
steps.stepSummary: The word means he is not punished until he has been 'shown' the reason, meaning he was warned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means he is not punished until he has been shown the reason of the matter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the word 'and sees.' It means the sinner must first be made to understand why the act is forbidden, and that is התראה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since 'seeing' cannot mean looking, the גמרא reads it as 'seeing' in the sense of understanding. The person must clearly know he is sinning, and that knowledge comes from being warned.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason of the matter: why the act is forbidden

phrases.english: Rather, until they show him
the reason of the matter.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא עַד שֶׁיַּרְאוּהוּ טַעְמוֹ שֶׁל דָּבָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 30 by reading 'וראה' as being shown the reason, meaning being warned.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of a word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'וראה' means physical seeing, which makes no sense for this sin.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'וראה' means being made to understand the reason, which is התראה.

steps.title: If it is not needed for כרת
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins an 'אם אינו ענין' argument: the warning lesson cannot be about כרת, so it must apply somewhere else.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is not needed for the matter of כרת,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. The פסוק speaks about כרת, but warning cannot be needed there, so the lesson must be moved to another punishment. The sentence finishes in the next section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: כרת is a punishment from Heaven, and Heaven knows whether the person sinned on purpose, so no warning is needed. The 'אם אינו ענין' method says that when a lesson cannot apply to its own topic, we apply it to a different topic.

keyTerms.meaning: If it does not apply to this topic. A method that moves a lesson to another topic
Spiritual cutting off, a punishment from Heaven

phrases.english: If it is not needed for the matter of excision —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins explaining how a warning rule found in a פסוק about כרת applies to punishments given by the court.
steps.terutzResolutionType: אם אינו ענין: moving the lesson to a different topic
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The warning lesson applies to the כרת mentioned in the פסוק itself.
steps.terutzMaskana: Warning is meaningless for כרת, so the lesson must apply elsewhere. This is completed in the next section.
